stories.topic: The Good Gyan folder he never opens
stories.summary: Twitter lets you sort bookmarks into folders, and Amit keeps one called 'Good Gyan' for tweets that strike him as wise. He saves them meaning to come back and be enlightened, then admits he never does. This episode was his way of finally putting the folder to use: he reads the tweets to Ajay, who has not seen them, and Ajay reacts on the spot.
stories.insight: What you save says as much about you as about the people who wrote it. Amit expects the folder to expose his own foibles, and Ajay sums it up: 'The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer.' Turning a private hoard into a conversation is one way to make bookmarking worth something.
stories.quote: Guess what? I never go back, I just bookmark and all of that.

stories.topic: Aanchal Malhotra, Partition, and Chinese whispers in the brain
stories.summary: While preparing for his episode with Aanchal Malhotra, who collected memories of Partition in a book, Amit learned that memory is not a file stored once and pulled up unchanged. Each time you remember something, you are recalling your last act of remembering it. That is why two people who shared a moment can later describe it in completely different ways.
stories.insight: Memory is rebuilt every time we use it, and it is shaped by who we are from the first impression onward. This was Amit's gloss on Anais Nin's line, and the lesson he draws is to be slow to judge.
stories.quote: The first time we remember it, we go back to that file. The next time we go back to the remembering of it, the next time we go back to the remembering of the remembering of it. And it's Chinese whispers all the way down.

stories.topic: Drifting toward Hawaii off Santa Cruz
stories.summary: A friend who teaches at UC Santa Cruz took Ajay and Ila out sailing. The wind began pushing the boat away from Santa Cruz, and Ajay realised that if they did nothing at all, the wind would carry them to Hawaii. His friend confirmed it. Ajay found it eerie that the boat could simply keep going forever on the wind.
stories.insight: Ajay told this in response to Faulkner's line about losing sight of the shore, and Amit teased him for taking the metaphor literally. The story still makes the metaphor felt: leaving the shore is unsettling because open water has no natural stopping point, and that is exactly why it takes courage.
stories.quote: You mean if we do absolutely nothing, the wind will just take this boat all the way out to Hawaii? And he said, Yeah, pretty much

stories.topic: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan and the all-vegetarian weekend
stories.summary: A Raja invited Bade Ghulam Ali Khan to give a Sunday concert. The singer arrived on Friday and was treated lavishly, except that every meal was vegetarian: Friday, Saturday and Sunday. After the concert the Raja told him that his performances elsewhere had been so magical the oceans seemed ready to part, but today's, though good, lacked that flavour. The maestro answered with a rhyming one-liner tying the quality of his singing to the food he had been given.
stories.insight: What goes in shapes what comes out. You cannot starve an artist of what feeds him and expect magic. Amit, a committed carnivore like Ajay, told it right after Ajay's 'restaurant, not a meadow' joke.
stories.quote: Today it was good, but it didn't quite have that flavor.

stories.topic: The WhatsApp group that ran on bitching
stories.summary: Amit was once in a WhatsApp group of people both he and Ajay know, where about ninety percent of the conversation was bitching about others, mutual friends included. He left. He later heard that they then bitched about him, which did not surprise him.
stories.insight: Groups of complainers keep sinking, and anyone who leaves becomes the next target. Amit's conclusion is to cut such people out as brutally as you can and spend your time with people who help you build ideas instead of tearing them down.
stories.quote: Like ninety percent of their talk was bitching about other people, including mutual friends. Like after I left the group they bitched about me.

stories.topic: A father's death and the missing medical data
stories.summary: Amit's father died in 2021 during the second COVID wave. He got talking with a friend who had just sold his company and had also lost his father. Amit concluded that the real failure was data: no one had a patient's full information in one place, and someone should build a startup to fix that. He has since heard of several people working on parts of the problem.
stories.insight: Personal grief led him to a systems problem. Consolidated records let a doctor, with consent, see the whole picture. Anonymised data across a whole population lets AI spot local disease patterns, such as something unusual in Sholapur, that no single doctor ever could. That is a public health gain, beyond individual care.
stories.quote: I just thought that the real problem here is in the data collection and having all the data.

stories.topic: From twenty-minute episodes to ten-hour ones
stories.summary: Amit started The Seen and the Unseen with twenty-minute episodes because the standard advice was that attention spans are short. He has since recorded oral-history-style episodes of eight, nine and even ten hours.
stories.insight: This is Faulkner's 'lose sight of the shore' in practice. Many of the rules we follow are inherited rather than tested, and good work often needs you to ignore them and trust yourself.
stories.quote: I would never have done that if I let the conventional thinking hold me down that oh, you know, short attention spans, do twenty minute episodes, which is how I started.

stories.topic: How Ajay writes his Business Standard column
stories.summary: Ajay has written a fortnightly Business Standard column since the mid-1990s, due on Sunday afternoon. When it goes well, he settles on the idea by Saturday evening, often after texting friends for suggestions. He then reads around the topic without taking notes or planning the argument, looking at data and graphs, and goes to sleep. On Sunday, between about ten and noon, he writes it with far more clarity.
stories.insight: A practical version of Amit's point about learning: load the question into your head, stop pushing, and let sleep connect the pieces. Amit, who wrote weekly columns for fifteen years, agrees that once the brain accepts a deadline, it finds a way.
stories.quote: Then I read a bit about that. I sort of fill my head with the question in a non-purposive way. Meaning I'm not trying to take notes or plan the storyline of the article.

stories.topic: The industrial policy paper that missed the point
stories.summary: Ajay recently came across an article on industrial policy for developing countries and was excited by it. He found it had been written by a narrow economist who had read only development economics papers and knew nothing of state capability or public choice theory. Yet the one distinctive thing about industrial policy in a poor country is that the state is far more likely to be out of control and to make mistakes.
stories.insight: This illustrates Shahab Bakhtiari's 'five meters away' rule. Specialists who never read outside their own corner write papers that miss the central issue, here the principal-agent problem between citizens and a weak state.
stories.quote: it just struck me that this was written by a narrow economist who had never really thought deeply about development, who had no understanding of state capability, who had not thought about public choice theory.

recommendations.item: Rashomon
recommendations.creator: Akira Kurosawa
recommendations.context: Amit's example while discussing Anais Nin's line on perception.
recommendations.reason: The same event is told from several points of view, each credible. It shows that perception depends on the perceiver, not that only one witness is telling the truth.

recommendations.item: Remnants of a Separation
recommendations.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a memorable book while recalling his episode with its author.
recommendations.reason: Aanchal Malhotra collected memories of Partition. Preparing for that conversation taught Amit how memory reshapes itself every time it is recalled.

recommendations.item: Memories and Things (Episode 195 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Aanchal Malhotra
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'this great episode I did with Aanchal Malhotra'.
recommendations.reason: The conversation that gave him the 'Chinese whispers all the way down' understanding of memory.

recommendations.item: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Episode 85 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the intro as the episode where they first argued about social media.
recommendations.reason: Round one of the debate this episode continues: Ajay sees Twitter as a cesspool, and Amit agrees but says a well-curated feed is a gift.

recommendations.item: Tweet quoting Anais Nin: 'We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.'
recommendations.creator: Anais Nin (shared by @gigi_dreamer)
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 1, on perception.
recommendations.reason: A reminder that we are part of whatever we perceive, so we should take a step back before judging. It set off the episode's first argument, with Ajay pushing back in defence of objective truth.

recommendations.item: Peyman Milanfar's tweet on reading old work
recommendations.creator: Peyman Milanfar
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 2: 'If you're a researcher in tech and you're not reading anything more than five years old, you can be sure your own work will be forgotten five years from now.'
recommendations.reason: Ajay agreed at once, since computer science keeps reinventing the same things badly. Amit added that understanding how a field developed gives you depth, even where the old work is now obsolete.

recommendations.item: Shahab Bakhtiari's quote tweet extending Milanfar's rule
recommendations.creator: Shahab Bakhtiari
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 3: the rule also applies spatially. If you read nothing five meters away from you, your work will be forgotten five meters away.
recommendations.reason: An argument for reading across disciplines and places. It ties to Ajay's complaint about American economists generalising from a study of Arizona to the whole world.

recommendations.item: Emacs
recommendations.context: Recalled from the UNIX episode while agreeing with Milanfar.
recommendations.reason: Ajay likes it because it is fifty years old. That age has produced elegant, clear design and bulletproof code, unlike today's disposable software.

recommendations.item: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points back to it on why old tools hold up.
recommendations.reason: Where he first explained why he values old, well-designed software like Emacs.

recommendations.item: Constraints & Creativity (Episode 90 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links it to the case for studying old computing.
recommendations.reason: Early computing was done under severe limits, such as landing Apollo on the moon with 64 KB of RAM. Those limits produced deep insight worth studying.

recommendations.item: Beware of Industrial Policy (Episode 89 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned before his critique of a narrow paper on industrial policy.
recommendations.reason: Background for why industrial policy in developing countries has to start from state capability and public choice theory.

recommendations.item: Ash Joglekar's tweet on solitary hobbies
recommendations.creator: Ash Joglekar
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 4, from a Facebook friend of two decades whom Amit has never met and who tweets 'wonderfully well about science'.
recommendations.reason: Reading, long-distance running and science give you a refuge from personal and world tragedies. Amit adds that they also create the solitude needed for self-reflection.

recommendations.item: Gurpriya Sidhu's tweet: 'Be like a coach or a comrade in your professional relationships. Be like a gardener in your personal ones.'
recommendations.creator: Gurpriya Sidhu
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 5, from a former student in her early twenties whose tweets often end up in his folder.
recommendations.reason: Work relationships have a function, while personal ones mean accepting people as they are. The tweet led to the gardener-versus-architect discussion of firms and novels.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining how learning happens.
recommendations.reason: Several modules teach learning how to learn, including the limited working memory that holds about four chunks, and why insight comes during downtime.

recommendations.item: Morgan Housel's tweet quoting Montesquieu on happiness
recommendations.creator: Morgan Housel
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 6: being happy is easy, but being happier than others is hard, because we believe others to be happier than they are.
recommendations.reason: A sharp diagnosis of envy, more relevant than ever now that social media pits our real lives against other people's curated ones.

recommendations.item: Morgan Housel's writing on money
recommendations.creator: Morgan Housel
recommendations.context: Amit teases Ajay for not having read him: 'You should read Morgan Housel.'
recommendations.reason: He is a writer on money whom Amit considers essential reading.

recommendations.item: Maya C Popa's tweet quoting William Faulkner, and her Twitter feed
recommendations.creator: Maya C Popa
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 7: 'You cannot swim for new horizons unless you have courage to lose sight of the shore.'
recommendations.reason: Amit calls her a poet and a fine poetry editor whose feed is 'awesome'. The line spoke to him because good work requires breaking from conventional thinking.

recommendations.item: Peyman Milanfar's tweet quoting Max Weber: 'I am not a donkey, I don't have a field.'
recommendations.creator: Peyman Milanfar
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 8, on breadth.
recommendations.reason: A one-line rebuke of academic silos, where someone can spend ten years on wheat production in 1853 Arizona and never see the bigger picture.

recommendations.item: What Economics Can Learn (Episode 75 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a great episode' on Vijayendra Rao's paper.
recommendations.reason: It examines how economics, sociology and anthropology have walled themselves off from each other, with further silos inside each.

recommendations.item: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
recommendations.creator: Vijayendra Rao
recommendations.context: The paper behind Episode 75, brought up under the Weber tweet.
recommendations.reason: It argues economics should look at itself more critically and stop working in isolation from neighbouring disciplines.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on whiners
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 9: stop complaining. Fix the problem, ask for help, or accept that griping only pollutes the atmosphere with bitterness.
recommendations.reason: Amit has made cutting out negativity close to a life mission. Ajay added that people should encourage new ideas at birth.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on grappling with complex issues
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 10: if a long-debated issue seems obvious and one side seems stupid or evil, you have shrunk the issue to fit your mind.
recommendations.reason: It diagnoses tribal thinking on questions that really are complex. Ajay objected that some debates, such as nationalism and militarism, are closed for him.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on what AI does to us
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 13: as we make machines more human-like, they make us more machine-like. The worry is not AI becoming conscious but humanity becoming unconscious.
recommendations.reason: It sharpens the case for using AI as a tool rather than a crutch.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal's Substack
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Amit calls Bhogal 'an absolutely fantastic thinker' and mentions his Substack.
recommendations.reason: Bhogal built his reputation on Twitter megathreads that combine existing knowledge into original insights and see the world very sharply.

recommendations.item: Visakan Veerasamy's tweet quoting Nietzsche: 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.'
recommendations.creator: Visakan Veerasamy
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 11, from 'one of the really interesting thinkers on Twitter', whom Amit is often urged to invite on his show.
recommendations.reason: It started the discussion about whether purpose brings happiness or a burden.

recommendations.item: Dylan O'Sullivan's tweet quoting Matt Kahn: 'People can only meet you as deeply as they've met themselves.'
recommendations.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 12, from a young curator whose literature tweets fill Amit's literature folder.
recommendations.reason: You understand others only as far as you understand yourself. Ajay adds that a good conversation takes a rich, mature mind.

recommendations.item: Dylan O'Sullivan's tweet quoting Schopenhauer on the art of not reading
recommendations.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
recommendations.context: Read alongside the Matt Kahn tweet.
recommendations.reason: To read good books you have to skip bad ones, starting with whatever the crowd is excited about this week, because life is short.

recommendations.item: Tiffany Ryder's tweet on insecure doctors
recommendations.creator: Tiffany Ryder
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 14, reacting to a clinic sign that read 'Please don't confuse your Google search with my medical degree.'
recommendations.reason: Her retort, that any doctor threatened by WebMD should have studied harder, raises the question of what expertise means when information is a click away.

recommendations.item: Lancelot Pinto's tweet on respecting patients
recommendations.creator: Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 15, Pinto's quote tweet agreeing with Ryder.
recommendations.reason: Patients know what they are going through better than anyone and are their own best advocates. Doctors should encourage them to read up instead of gaslighting them.

recommendations.item: Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Amit mentions 'a great episode with Lancelot' about the practice of medicine.
recommendations.reason: Pinto is one of the rare doctors who reads papers daily, and the episode covers medical practice in general.

recommendations.item: Sahil Bloom's tweet: 'Preparation always beats planning.'
recommendations.creator: Sahil Bloom
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 16: planning expects order, preparation expects chaos.
recommendations.reason: Amit first took Bloom for a self-help tweeter, then noticed how many of his tweets he was bookmarking.

recommendations.item: Sahil Bloom's book on the five kinds of wealth
recommendations.creator: Sahil Bloom
recommendations.context: Bought and sitting on Amit's Kindle, unread at the time of recording.
recommendations.reason: A new book from a thinker Amit has come to rate highly. He expected to have read it by the time the episode aired.

recommendations.item: Lynk's tweet on crackheads
recommendations.creator: Lynk
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 17, 'one of my favorite tweets of all time' from someone Amit knows nothing about.
recommendations.reason: Crackheads never say they are too broke to smoke tonight. They get up and make it happen. If you want something badly enough, you find a way.

recommendations.item: Pico Iyer's tweet quoting Rousseau on wisdom
recommendations.creator: Pico Iyer
recommendations.context: Good Gyan 18: wisdom is knowing which things are necessary, less necessary and completely unnecessary to know. Iyer adds that for that, you have to put your phone away.
recommendations.reason: The episode's closing lesson in curation, which Amit immediately turned on Ajay.

recommendations.item: Paul Graham's essays
recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Amit's sign-off recommendation, with his essays page linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Graham's tweets often land in Amit's Good Gyan folder, and Amit rates him as one of the greatest essayists ever: 'Just marvelous. Absolutely marvelous.'

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes and not discussed on air.
recommendations.reason: A long-form conversation with Ajay. It fits his remark here that, having lived through the 20th century, he treats debates about nationalism and militarism as closed.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit agrees that social media went bad when retweets and likes began amplifying tribalism and the hunger for validation. But a well-curated feed lets you listen to the world's best minds think aloud every morning, sometimes even in dialogue with each other. Bookmark folders turn that stream into a personal library.
core_ideas.quote: if you curate your feed well, you are actually getting the privilege to listen to the best minds in the world think aloud for your benefit every morning, some of them even engaging in dialogue, which is masterful.

core_ideas.explanation: Anais Nin's line is about perception rather than reality. Chairs are real, but how we read people, relationships and complex events depends on who we are. Memory adds another layer of distortion because it is rebuilt each time it is recalled. The practical lesson is humility: on anything too complex to fully grasp, keep open the possibility that you are wrong.
core_ideas.quote: it should be a caution to us to not rush to judgment all the time, to not draw easy conclusions, to sort of be open, always take a step back, and be aware that we are part of the equation

core_ideas.concept: Attach a degree of confidence to everything you believe
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay objects to the post-truth idea that everyone has their own truth, which opens the door to every conspiracy theory. Some knowledge is certain, like Planck's formula for black body radiation, which is correct to the last decimal. How social media changed the world is much fuzzier. The real skill is calibrating how sure you are about each belief while continuing the uphill search for truth, which is what separates us from cats.
core_ideas.quote: learning how to attach uncertainty around each of the things that we think are true.

core_ideas.concept: Learn a field in the order it developed
core_ideas.explanation: Old work matters even when it is obsolete. Learning the sequence of puzzle, crisis and solution builds deep understanding. Philosophy has barely moved since Plato, and even a physicist gains from going back to Newton. Old engineering was often done under brutal constraints, such as Apollo's 64 KB of RAM, which forced deep insight. Without this history, fields like computer science keep reinventing the same things badly.
core_ideas.quote: So we've discussed on other occasions the best way to learn a field is to learn it in historical sequence.

core_ideas.explanation: Interdisciplinary work is more than a hunt for unclaimed ground at the edges of fields. Understanding the world takes history, geography and neighbouring disciplines, and breadth makes your work matter to more people. Max Weber's 'I am not a donkey, I don't have a field' sums up the case against silos.
core_ideas.quote: If you narrowly write papers on superconductivity, they'll only be read by the superconductivity gang.

core_ideas.concept: Solitude for reflection, company for sparks
core_ideas.explanation: Amit sees too little self-reflection in the world, and even our time alone is swallowed by screens. Solitary hobbies give that reflection room. Ajay values long, quiet mountain walks, but says his research has always needed other people to argue with, persuade and fail to persuade, in a setting where it is safe to make mistakes.
core_ideas.quote: There is not enough self reflection in the world. And you can only reflect on yourself when you spend time with yourself.

core_ideas.explanation: Gurpriya Sidhu suggests being a coach or comrade at work and a gardener with the people you love. The metaphor also fits novel-writing: architects plan every room before building, while gardeners start with overgrowth and prune until a shape emerges, which Amit thinks is how most great novelists work. It fits firms too: one view runs a firm like cooking, mixing ingredients from the top down, while the other creates conditions where many attempts can bloom or fail.
core_ideas.quote: a firm is a little more like gardening, that you create conditions and there are many things being attempted, and some of them bloom and some of them don't, and you don't necessarily do central planning within the firm.

core_ideas.concept: Envy, and the healthy selfishness that cures it
core_ideas.explanation: Montesquieu says happiness is easy but being happier than others is hard, because we overestimate how happy they are. Social media makes this worse by pitting our real lives against other people's curated ones. Ajay's cure is to stay absorbed in your own work of writing, making and building, which leaves no room for envy. Amit adds Naval Ravikant's test: before envying someone, ask whether you would take their whole life as a package, not just the part you admire.
core_ideas.quote: It's like I am on my selfish project of make me. Then why am I so bothered about you?

core_ideas.explanation: Focused study uses a small working memory that holds about four chunks, so forcing it leads to frustration. Insight comes later, while you relax or sleep and different parts of the brain make connections. So schedule free time deliberately instead of packing your calendar, and do what Ajay does with his column: fill your head with the question, then sleep on it.
core_ideas.quote: The learning happens where you're chilling, you're not even thinking about it consciously. Maybe you're sleeping.

core_ideas.concept: Don't whine, and back ideas when they are new
core_ideas.explanation: Gurwinder Bhogal's rule is to fix the problem, ask for help, or stop complaining, because complaining only spreads bitterness. Ajay adds the positive side: when someone shares a new idea, support it first and save the fifteen criticisms for later, because we are shaped by how others respond to our ideas. Amit notes that harsh feedback lands differently on different people. He has often seen men take it as a personal insult and women turn it on themselves through impostor syndrome, so it pays to think about how you deliver it.
core_ideas.quote: emotional encouragement is just so disproportionately important at the point of inception.

core_ideas.concept: Don't shrink an issue to fit your mind
core_ideas.explanation: If people have argued about something for ages and you find the answer obvious, you have probably reduced it to a tribal script. Choosing the tribal line on a genuinely complex question shows you care more about your side than about the truth. Ajay notes that some questions, such as nationalism and militarism, he personally regards as settled, even though many people still champion them.
core_ideas.quote: the moment you take the tribal line, You are in a sense confessing that you have reduced yourself to tribalism and you don't really care about the truth.

core_ideas.concept: Purpose is powerful, but don't cling to outcomes
core_ideas.explanation: Nietzsche's 'why' makes almost any 'how' bearable. Practical problems can be solved, but the fire has to come from you. Amit asks whether purpose actually brings happiness. Ajay answers with the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, but you do not control outcomes. If you measure a big purpose only by its results, you set yourself up for pain, because the world owes you nothing.
core_ideas.quote: Purpose is the superpower Everything else is solvable.

core_ideas.concept: Wisdom means knowing what to ignore
core_ideas.explanation: Schopenhauer's art of not reading and Rousseau's definition of wisdom make the same point. Real wisdom is sorting things into necessary, less necessary and completely unnecessary to know, and skipping whatever the crowd is excited about this week. Pico Iyer adds that you cannot do this without putting your phone away.
core_ideas.quote: Real wisdom is not the knowledge of everything, but the knowledge of which things in life are necessary, which are less necessary, and which are completely unnecessary to know.

core_ideas.concept: Use AI as a tool, not a crutch
core_ideas.explanation: Bhogal warns that outsourcing our thinking makes us more machine-like. Ajay is not worried, because he believes creativity comes from deep inside the human mind and AI will just take over tasks. Amit, an AI optimist, gives the same caveat he would give for any technology: use it to extend your own thinking, not to replace it.
core_ideas.quote: don't let it become a crutch. Let it be a tool.

core_ideas.concept: Informed patients, and AI to make up for doctor shortages
core_ideas.explanation: Patients who research their conditions are allies. Ajay's worry is that most Indian doctors do not read the medical literature. Amit adds that in fields like nutrition, old training can be not just outdated but harmful. Ajay's hope is a new model: nurses spend hours compiling a complete patient history, and that file goes to an AI. Research suggests that, given a full formal history, AI beats almost all doctors, which could be India's way to solve both the quantity and quality of doctors.
core_ideas.quote: when the complete patient history is given to the AI in a formal way, it beats almost all the doctors of the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Plans assume order and break at the first punch. Preparation assumes chaos and becomes second nature through years of practice. Ajay says good military planning is valuable because it rehearses many scenarios, logistics and the fact that the opponent also gets a say, which readies the mind even after the plan itself fails.
core_ideas.quote: planning is based on the expectation of order. Preparation is based on the expectation of chaos.

core_ideas.concept: Want it badly enough, or don't do it
core_ideas.explanation: From Lynk's crackhead tweet: people who really want something find a way. When aspiring writers ask Amit whether they should write a book, his answer is no, because anyone who truly wanted to would already be writing. Wanting can be cultivated, and remembering that your time is limited is one way to do it.
core_ideas.quote: Because if you need to ask, the answer is no. You have to want it badly enough, so you're just going to do it.

core_ideas.explanation: Faulkner's line is about clearing conventional thinking out of the way, the way Amit's podcast grew from twenty minutes to ten hours. Ajay adds his own: 'A headful of fears has no space for dreams.' Asked which oceans he has fallen in love with, Ajay says he never stayed stuck in one field and always moved to the next adjacent one.
core_ideas.quote: So you sometimes have to let go of the shore, and you sometimes just have to have faith in yourself

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens the episode by throwing down the gauntlet: 'Amit, you have once claimed to me that Twitter is more than the cesspool of the global mind. Prove it.'
Ajay on why we should keep pursuing truth: otherwise 'you might as well, you know, be a cat. So cats have no upward journey of figuring out the spectrum of black body radiation.'

Amit ends the perception argument by insisting on agreement: 'Of course I agree with you, and of course you agree with me, right? Right? Right, Ajay? You agree with me, right? Don't mess with me, just agree with me.'
Ajay: 'But I mean novelists don't start with a spreadsheet of all the characters and their characteristics.' Amit: 'Oh my God, this is what you would do, isn't it? Please remain an economist.'
Ajay on his love of mountain walks: 'I'm so out of breath that mostly I can't talk,' so the walks turn into long, quiet meditation by default.

After the Weber tweet, Ajay recalls the film Ninotchka. A humourless Russian communist in a Paris restaurant orders boiled cabbage and beet, and the waiter replies: 'Ma'am, this is a restaurant, not a meadow.'

Ajay brings back a one-liner from when Facebook's market cap overtook Google's: 'knowing everyone is worth more than knowing everything.' Amit: 'This is brilliant, but on Facebook you don't know everyone, and Google you don't know everything.'
Ajay's AI summary of Schopenhauer's art of not reading: 'Don't follow anybody on Twitter.' Amit, in the middle of a Twitter-sourced episode: 'All these are from Twitter. Don't mess with me, man.'

Amit teases Ajay about the sailboat story: when the tweet was literal, Ajay read it as a metaphor, and when Faulkner was clearly being metaphorical, Ajay answered with a shore that was literally moving away.
Amit on pulmonologist Lancelot Pinto's book in progress: it will still be read fifty years from now, 'but the fucker has to write it first.'

Ajay's six tiers of medical literacy: 'Doctor that uses Google Scholar. Doctor that uses Google, doctor that uses nothing, patient that uses Google Scholar, patient that uses Google, patient that uses nothing.'
As daylight fades during the shoot, Amit falls back on their own earlier episode: 'Ajay, you know the light is going. We've done an episode on constraints. Great things happen despite constraints.'
After Amit's 'think like a dope head who wants crack', Ajay offers 'a useless tweet' in reply: 'cocaine is nature's way of saying you have too much money.'

After the Pico Iyer line about putting your phone away, Amit points at Ajay, who 'is laughing because he's fucking guilty', having spent half an hour before the shoot taking calls about the markets and America. Amit then improvises a Beatles-style lyric: 'Hey, you gotta hide that phone away.'

Amit on Ajay's erratic recommendation habits, which swing between zero and seven: 'luckily there's no scope for you giving minus seven recommendations. You take away seven things from the readers' heads.'
Amit, explaining working memory, takes a dig at 'the Monty Hall problem which you are still refusing to grok.'
Amit quotes Joan Robinson: whatever you truthfully say about India, the opposite is also true. He adds that the same applies to much of the world.
Ajay uses the line 'If you prick us, do we not bleed?' to argue that some realities are shared by all seven billion people and are not matters of opinion.
Ajay's one-liner capturing the zero-sum mindset: 'It is not enough to win, others have to lose.' He follows it with: 'Resentment is like taking poison and hoping the other person dies.'
Amit cites Jonathan Haidt's work on how competing with other people's projected selves on social media has particularly harmed young teenage girls.

Amit suggests the Chinese team behind DeepSeek built competitive models at a fraction of Western costs because they understood the past and worked well within their constraints. Ajay cites Apollo landing on the moon with 64 KB of RAM.
Ajay offers the prayer he attributes to 'maybe some Christian sources': strength to change what I can, serenity to accept what I can't, and the wisdom to know the difference.

On planning: Mike Tyson's 'Everybody has a plan until they are punched in the mouth', plus 'Once the shooting starts, the plan is useless, but the planning is everything' (Ajay admits 'I forget who' said it). Amit imagines Tyson's plan for Lennox Lewis falling apart after the first punch.
Amit recalls a 1980s Japanese saying from the days of expensive Kodak film and manual cameras: 'if you want to make a man a pauper, give him a camera.'
